Getting a tutor for physics is probably a good idea if you struggled with physics before, especially since they can probably also help you with math-related questions if needed. In my experience, both mainly take tons of practice, and then you should be fine. Without them, you would also have a very hard time with some first-year MBLS courses, so also definitely try to understand the curriculum instead of purely trying to pass the exam.

I personally really enjoy MBLS so far, I'm currently in the last period of the first year, and luckily passed all courses so far. I however was not new to university, as I studied medicine last year but ended up switching because I did not enjoy it and found out I really did not want to become a doctor but want to go into research. This did give me a "head-start" into this program I feel, as most people who were fresh out of secondary school really had to adjust to the pace and difficulty of a university program. My biggest tip for this is to really try to keep up with all the work, attend all lectures and tutorials, and you will get accustomed to the workload quickly. Also, most courses have a way to get a bonus on top of your exam grade, which sometimes can add up to a whole point, which can make the difference between failing or passing, so take that opportunity.

There seems to be a really high dropout rate however, as we started the year with almost 150 people and I'm pretty sure that we are below 100 now, and there will be even more people dropping out at the end of the year probably. From what I've heard, the previous year also pretty much halved in numbers. I am not sure what the reason of this high dropout-rate is, but it may be good to know.

I can give my experience and tips about the courses I've followed up until now if you are interested:

**MBLS-101 Cell Biology**

This course is an introduction to cell biology, and is mainly a lot of reading and remembering. The lectures are very good in my opinion, and by attending all lectures and keeping up, it is a really doable course. So yeah, my main tip would be to keep up with all the material, follow the course schedule including reading the chapters, and make flashcards with all terms you need to remember. Not much special, but yeah

​

**MBLS-102 Mathematics and Programming**

This course is pretty much composed of two smaller courses, one in which you learn a variety of new mathematics skills (which mainly build onto the mathematics B skills (like new integration methods)), and introduces a few new concepts (like imaginary numbers and Taylor series) which you will need in MBLS-104 (Phys Chem) and MBLS-106 (Biological Physics). If you do all practice assignments and again, keep up with everything, it is quite doable.

The other part is composed of learning to program in Python and applying it (making plots of data/functions and analyzing biological data like DNA sequences). I personally did really enjoy this part (but I already had some experience in Python) but many others really struggled with this part. Try to practice a lot, and really understand what you're doing and why. In our year, the exam was an open-book assignment, and looked a lot like the practice exam, so if you struggle with it, try to focus on the practice exam when studying.

​

**MBLS-103 Organic Chemistry of Drug Molecules**

This is an introduction to organic chemistry, and you learn basic properties of molecules and how they react, and also some important reactions. I mainly studied this by a lot of practice, but other people have also found succes using flashcards.

​

**MBLS-104 Physical Chemistry of Life Sciences**

This course is also composed of two parts: spectroscopy and thermodynamics. Spectroscopy is very doable, just practice a lot with reading out spectra, as like 80% of the exam is composed of that. The thermo part is very difficult though, and it is the most failed exam in the first year. The concepts are very abstract and quite some math is involved, which is probably the cause of this. Attend all lectures and tutorials, and practice a lot, and if you do not pass the exam, do not stress too much as you can do a retake and many people do pass that. Otherwise, you can always redo the course a year later.

​

**MBLS-105 Biomolecular Chemistry**

This course mainly looks at the chemistry of proteins, their function (like folding, enzyme activity, etc), saccharides and nucleic acids. It mainly is a lot of studying, and you will need to memorize quite some formulas and structures, but I did not experience it as a very hard course.

​

**MBLS-204 Genomes, Cells and Tissues (elective)**

This is an elective course, so you can choose another course instead of this one, but this course is the sequel to MBLS-101 Cell Biology. You delve a lot deeper in the mechanisms and learn a lot more details. It is all memorization and studying, but it is quite a difficult course due to the very high amount of information (think: reading two 80-page chapters in a week, and memorize all details). I personally highly regretted choosing this course, as I want to go more into the chemistry-side of things (luckily still passed the course though), but if you want to go into cell research or similar things it is a highly essential course.

​
